posts.author: zipsister
posts.content_md:
I have been using my own developer for the last three years which is extremely active requiring much shorter exposure times than others (JD-2, JD-4, Pyro, etc). Used it for reflection and transmission on Slavich (especially VPR-M) and Agfa films and plates (8E75/56). Sometimes EDTA and sometimes Dichromates bleaches: 

Zip1:

Metol 1gr, 

Hydroquinone 1gr,

Phenidone 0.5gr, 

Sodium Sulphite 30gr, 

Ascorbic Acid 10gr, 

Potassium Hydroxide 30gr, 

water to make 1 litre

Dave

posts.author: jsfisher
posts.content_md: What sort of shelf life are you getting for it?

posts.author: zipsister
posts.content_md: I usually have used it up after about 3-4 months and it does start getting darker/oxidizing by then, BUT it still appears to be working as effectively right to the end. What I like about this formula is that it is extremely active reducing my exposure times drastically while retaining contrast and brightness of my work. I wouldn't use anything else now and haven't for years. Used it on the kilometre long Hololujah hologram which required 2 minute exposures for 1.1x1 metre hologram panels.if you only occasionally make holograms then just make up smaller quantities. If your exposure time is 30 seconds with your regular developer then start with 2 seconds with this formula.

posts.author: Arturo
posts.content_md:
Hi, I was wondering how safe is it (the components, I mean) for handling and mixing?

Thanks

posts.author: zipsister
posts.content_md: As safe as any other developer. I usually wear gloves regardless when mixing any chemicals just out of respect for my hands. Possasium Hydroxide will generate heat when the water goes in so I usually throw that chemical into the mix after the water has gone into my Pyrex container. But even if you don't the amount of water (1000ml) cools things almost immediately. These are all easily obtained chemicals, as well in an era when some are becoming hard to get or you need to take out another mortgage to buy them.

posts.author: zipsister
posts.content_md: Because I don't work like most in that I'm primarily working with very large holograms, even some of my test strips are metre square size then I tend to use this developer up fairly quickly and usually mix it up in four litre batches. But when making smaller holograms I would suggest placing some in your developer tray and using it over and over in the one session then dispose of what's left using fresh mixture for each session. Just a suggestion.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: Judging by the subject of your ISDH talk, you seem to be making transmissions. If so, have you used this developer on reflections? If you have, does this increase in speed also hold for reflections? Any idea why it's so much better? I'm also curious about the linearity of your reconstructions. It seems to me that a developer so fast as to be over 90% more efficient than standard developers (I believe you state that a 30 sec development time can be reduced to 2 seconds) would find it difficult to reconstruct the finer aspects of the sinusoid.

posts.author: zipsister
posts.content_md: Yes, I've used it for reflections in place of the pyro developer and with the dichromate bleach. It also over comes the hassle of accidently getting stained fingers with the pyro developer if you forget to put the rubber gloves on. The main benefit I've found is that the image brightness is on a par with the other developers with the bonus of shorter exposures. The mix of the Metol, Hydroquinone and Phenidone with the Potassium Hydroxide is quite an active combo. I'm not really surprised and certainly these chemicals are cheaper than pyro and catechol..

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
Yes, that does seem very aggressive. This looks like a combination of AAC and a metol-hydroquinone developer with pot hydroxide thrown in; although I'm not an expert on developers. I recall one time that the local store did not have any D19. The store owner told me that D76 with the addition of pot hydroxide would convert the D76 to D19. The altered D76 behaved just as I'd expect D19 to behave. I assume that both in your developer and the altered D76, the agressiveness of the developer is increased by the presence of the pot hydroxide. 

> **zipsister:** It also over comes the hassle of accidently getting stained fingers with the pyro developer if you forget to put the rubber gloves on

So true! I met some friends after a full day of using the pyro process, with my fingers a dirty brown colour. I recall I was given a lecture on the evils of smoking!

posts.author: John Sonley
posts.content_md: Dave, I seem to recall that you have a variation of your brew that separates the developer into Part A and Part B which are mixed in equal quantities before development - I guess the pot. hydroxide is the main component to be separated from the rest - probably improves shelf life?

posts.author: zipsister
posts.content_md:
John,

I used to split the mix but now keep it as a single mixture, but yes, separating them will no doubt extend the shelf life if you don't use it often. If you do split the mix make up the A part in 500ml of water and the Sodium Hydroxide in 500ml of water so that together they make the original strength solution.

Dave
